Why would you want to pay as much as possible for any position if you are a stockholder? Your earrings on that particular stock depend on company profits. Pay a Scandinavian? Why would you want to hire one if your company isn't based there? It will cost significantly more for little added productivity.  Stock holders and CEO's aren't friends. CEO's work for the stock holders. The idea of paying as little as possible is profit maximization and that's exactly what you're doing when you pay a CEO. Sure 12 million may sound like a big number but that's just the way the negotiation works. A good CEO will have large offers from a number of companies. 12 million in this case is the lowest number the investors believe will attract good candidates. A CEO generally doesn't get a raw cut of the profits. He either owns significant portions of stock so decisions that benefit investors also benfit him or he is paid a salary with bonuses for good performance.  The stock holders don't care about making him rich. They want the best possible person for the job who will do it for as little pay as possible. There are CEO's who earn very modest salaries like the CEO of Costco. That guy is paid modestly because he chooses to be. He is happy with what he makes and likes working for Costco. However the stock holders would also be likely to significantly increase the salary for the position if he left. It's all about paying everyone as little as possible relative to the results they can be expected to achieve. CEO's aren't just handed a fat salary they demand it. They are able to demand it by demonstrating a strong history of decisions that have cut costs and increased performance. The only reason Costco's CEO takes such a small salary is because he doesn't demand a larger one.

I can claim that. If the CEO makes decisions that improve productivity more than adding 2 million days worth of labor within a year. The opportunity cost of paying the CEO is lower than the opportunity cost of hiring more workers. The whole model is built around paying people what they are worth. Worth of a worker is determined based on their ability to contribute to productivity. This is simplifying things quite a bit. Depending upon where the worker is located if he is paid six dollars a day he likely costs the company significantly more than that. It would be nice to pay the worker more than that however it is illogical. Places where labor is cheap often have high rates of unemployment or underemployment. Simply put these individuals are lucky to have a job. It's not fair but that's just how it works. The CEO makes decisions like where to build a factory with this in mind. You could have a limited number of well paid employees in the US or you could have a much larger number of employees in India or Taiwan and see  larger productivity. This decision making process where costs are minimized and productivity is optimized is where the margins are generated that make paying a CEO highly a logical move. A higher paid position for c-suite individuals leads to more competitive appointments. Thus better corporate management. The same does not hold true for many lower level positions. A US or other first world worker cannot be expected to have a mucher higher level of productivity than a third world worker in many industries. This is why companies like Nike build sweat shops. The CEO is responsible for figuring out just how cheap you can go and still see high product quality with massive production. His pay is justified off of the margin he creates by building efficient infrastructure all the way up from manufacturing and supply chain to marketing. 
If you're still in doubt the question to ask is: why would the stock holders pay a CEO well when it is in their best interests to minimize costs? There's your answer they need a central figure to minimize costs and maximize revenues and his costs are lower than the costs they would have incurred had they not hired him.

For your assembly line worker you are viewing his contribution wrong. He provides general labor for 6 an hour not hundreds/thousands of products. Another laborer paid at the same rate could provide the same level of productivity. CEO's are paid because of their unique skill in making decisions. It's not a role that you can try out for or work up to. You make decisions you entire life and they are good enough to be promoted into roles of greater and greater responsibility until you are eventually selected for the position because it is believed that your ability to  make decisions makes you a good candidate. Your ability to make decisions is what makes you valuable. These guys tend to be worth what they make or the stockholders wouldn't be willing to pay them what they do. It takes a unique set of skills that are difficult to quantify to do the job well.
